newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM apologises over radiation leak.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM apologises over radiation leak.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto apologised to the nation on Wednesday for delays in reporting details of a fire and explosion that caused a radiation leak from Japan's only nuclear reprocessing plant.
"I apologise for the fact that the accident caused unnecessary concern among citizens," Hashimoto told parliament.

The fire and explosion occurred on Tuesday at a bituminisation facility for low-level nuclear waste inside a complex which houses a plant for reprocessing spent nuclear fuel at Tokaimura, 160 km (100 miles) north-east of Tokyo.
The plant, which has been shut, reprocesses about 12 percent of spent nuclear fuel from Japanese nuclear power plants with the rest sent overseas, mainly to France.
The fire exposed a total of 21 workers to very small amounts of radiation, a spokesman for the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corporation (PNC) said.
Some radiation leaked from the plant as a result of the accident but the operators said the amount was minimal and it soon dissipated, posing no risk to the public.

The accident was the latest blow to Japan's ambitious nuclear power programme, the subject of widespread public distrust after a 1995 cover-up of an accident at the country's only fast-breeder reactor, Monju.
Hashimoto said PNC should have been aware of the need for quick and accurate reports over any accident at nuclear plants following the incident at Monju, also run by the PNC.

"What I regret most is the fact that the PNC did not provide an adequate and speedy report on the fire and the radiation leak, after having been exposed to severe public criticism of its conduct over the Monju affair," Hashimoto told an Upper House budget committee session.
The facility in question is used to harden low-level irradiated liquid waste, a by-product from the main nuclear fuel reprocessing plant nearby, by mixing it with asphalt for storage in drums.
The complex is located in the cradle of Japan's nuclear power industry which supplies one-third of the country's electricity.

The fire, followed 10 hours later by a mysterious explosion, briefly set off a nuclear scare before officials determined that radiation levels were safe and the contaminated workers were given a clean bill of health and allowed to go home.
The force of the explosion blew out a steel door sealing the bituminisation facility and damaged coolant pipes and ventilation ducts, a PNC spokesman said on Wednesday.
"The focus of our probe is the reason for the latter explosion," the PNC spokesman told a news conference.

The incident happened on a day when Japan's nuclear programme was buffeted by the withdrawal of plans to build a new nuclear plant because of local opposition and environmental groups announced protests next week against a British ship carrying radioactive waste to Japan.
Kyushu Electric Power Company, one of Japan's 10 power companies, said on Tuesday it was abandoning a plan to build a nuclear plant in the southern city of Kushima because of strong local opposition.

Also on Tuesday, the environmental group Greenpeace announced protests next Tuesday against the arrival at a Japanese port on that date of a British freighter carrying about 20 tonnes of radioactive waste from France.
The cargo, which has drawn protests from countries on the ship's route, is the second shipment of waste being returned to Japan after processing by French state company COGEMA.
